c.tagline: Brazil's boundless concrete jungle that never sleeps.

emergency.note: Fire brigade is 193; English-speaking operators are rare, so have a Portuguese speaker or translation app ready.

avoid.reason: Open-air drug scene around Luz/centre — avoid.
Central districts empty out at night; pickpocketing and robbery — stay alert.

hood_desc: Vila Madalena is São Paulo's bohemian creative quarter, packed with street art, indie galleries, bars and buzzing nightlife, ideal for younger travelers and artists who want an energetic, walkable scene.
Jardins is the upscale, leafy district of luxury boutiques, fine dining and elegant tree-lined streets, best suited to affluent visitors seeking refined shopping and a polished, safe base.
Pinheiros is a trendy, foodie-forward neighborhood full of stylish restaurants, cafes, design shops and craft bars, appealing to hip professionals and creatives who like a lively yet livable vibe.

Itaim Bibi is a modern business and financial hub with sleek high-rises, upscale restaurants and vibrant after-work nightlife, great for business travelers and those wanting nightlife near corporate offices.

Liberdade is the historic Japanese and East Asian district known for its lanterns, Asian markets, ramen shops and weekend street fairs, perfect for travelers drawn to culture, food and a distinctive atmosphere on a budget.
lodging: INNSiDE by Meliá São Paulo Iguatemi

water.note: Tap water is technically treated but most visitors stick to bottled or filtered water as a precaution.

transit.pay: Use the rechargeable Bilhete Único card, sold at metro/CPTM stations and bus terminals, or simply tap a contactless Visa/Mastercard at the turnstiles and on most buses. A single Metro or CPTM ride costs about R$5.40 and a bus ride about R$5.30 (each roughly $1.05), with a discounted transfer between bus and rail within about 3 hours.
transit.hours: The Metro and CPTM run from around 4:40am to midnight, extended to about 1am on Fridays, Saturdays and pre-holidays; select 24-hour night bus lines cover key corridors when the rail network is closed.

transit.m: CPTM Line 13-Jade airport train to Engenheiro Goulart, connect to metro ~45 min
Municipal bus route 257 to Metro Tatuape ~55 min
Airport Bus Service executive coach to city center/Paulista ~50-70 min

food.name: Sanduiche de mortadela
food.desc: A soft roll packed with a towering pile of warm sliced mortadella and melted cheese - the city's most famous market bite.

places.name: Bar do Mane
places.note: Market stall serving the original stuffed mortadella sandwich since 1933.

places.name: Hocca Bar
places.note: The other Mercadao counter locals queue at for mortadella and pastel.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Pinheiros
places.note: Quieter market alternative with the same classic sandwich, fewer crowds.

food.name: Pastel de feira
food.desc: Thin fried pastry parcels stuffed with cheese, meat or palm heart, eaten hot at a street market with sugarcane juice.

places.name: Feira da Praca Benedito Calixto
places.note: Saturday street fair where the pastel stall is a Paulistano institution.

places.name: Hocca Bar
places.note: Famous for the outsized pastel de bacalhau, salt cod and all.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Pinheiros
places.note: Weekend fair stalls frying pastel to order alongside caldo de cana.

food.name: Virado a paulista
food.desc: The city's signature plate: bean puree, rice, kale, pork chop, sausage, fried egg, banana and crackling - traditionally a Monday lunch.

places.name: Bar da Dona Onca
places.note: Michelin-listed bar whose Monday virado is the benchmark version.

places.name: Salada Record
places.note: Old-school downtown lunch counter serving virado every single day.

places.name: Boteco Original
places.note: Busy neighbourhood boteco known for a generous Monday virado plate.

food.name: Pizza paulistana
food.desc: Sao Paulo's own thin-but-sturdy pizza with a generous topping load, a legacy of the city's huge Italian community.

places.name: Cantina e Pizzaria Speranza
places.note: Running since 1958 in the Italian quarter; the margherita is the order.

places.name: Pizza da Mooca
places.note: Ranked 5th in 50 Top Pizza Latin America 2025; book well ahead.

places.name: Veridiana
places.note: Top-100-in-the-world pizzeria in a grand old townhouse setting.

food.name: Coxinha
food.desc: Teardrop-shaped croquette of shredded chicken in dough, breaded and deep fried - the default Brazilian bar snack.

places.name: Veloso Bar
places.note: Award-winning coxinha with catupiry cheese; pair with a caipirinha.

places.name: Frango Assado da Freguesia (Frango)
places.note: Legendary neighbourhood bar famed for its fried bar snacks.

places.name: Bar Brahma
places.note: Historic 1948 corner bar; classic petiscos with live music at night.

food.name: Feijoada
food.desc: Slow-cooked black bean and pork stew served with rice, collards, farofa and orange - the weekend blowout meal.

places.name: Bolinha
places.note: Serves its famous feijoada every day, a Sao Paulo tradition for decades.

places.name: Bar da Dona Onca
places.note: Saturday feijoada in the Copan building; arrive early for a table.

places.name: Bar Brahma
places.note: Old-guard downtown bar with a reliable weekend feijoada spread.

food.name: Caipirinha
food.desc: Brazil's national cocktail: cachaca muddled with lime and sugar over ice, simple and dangerously drinkable.

places.name: Bar da Dona Onca
places.note: Its caipirinhas are as praised as the food; try the fruit variations.

places.name: Bar Brahma
places.note: Classic downtown bar, a good spot for a caipirinha with live samba.

places.name: Boteco Original
places.note: Cachaca-focused boteco with a long list of premium pours.

food.name: Caldo de cana
food.desc: Freshly pressed sugarcane juice, often with a squeeze of lime or pineapple - the standard partner to a market pastel.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Juice presses run all day beside the pastel and sandwich counters.

places.name: Feira da Praca Benedito Calixto
places.note: Weekend fair stall pressing cane to order; cheap and ice cold.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Pinheiros
places.note: Quieter market with cane juice next to the pastel stands.

landmarks: Sé Cathedral (Catedral da Sé)
This grand neo-Gothic cathedral anchors Praça da Sé, the historic heart of São Paulo, and is one of the largest Gothic-style churches in the world.
Museu de Arte de São Paulo (MASP)
Famous for its bold red concrete-and-glass structure suspended above an open public plaza on Avenida Paulista, MASP houses Latin America's premier art collection.
Edifício Copan
Designed by Oscar Niemeyer, this sinuous wave-shaped skyscraper is one of the most photographed and recognizable silhouettes on the São Paulo skyline.
Museu do Ipiranga (Museu Paulista)
This palatial 19th-century museum marks the site where Brazil's independence was declared and offers sweeping formal gardens plus panoramic city views.
Ibirapuera Park
São Paulo's largest and most beloved urban park, featuring Niemeyer-designed pavilions, lakes, and the iconic curved Oca and Marquise structures, ideal for photography and relaxation.
Theatro Municipal de São Paulo
A opulent Belle Époque opera house modeled on the Paris Opéra, its ornate facade and interior make it a top spot for classic architectural photos.
Avenida Paulista
The city's most iconic avenue, lined with skyscrapers, museums, and cultural venues, it embodies São Paulo's dynamic urban energy.
Mercado Municipal de São Paulo (Mercadão)
A stunning stained-glass-domed market hall famous for its mortadella sandwiches and vibrant produce stalls, a feast for both the palate and the camera.
Beco do Batman (Batman's Alley)
A vibrant open-air graffiti alley in Vila Madalena packed with ever-changing street art, making it one of the city's most Instagrammed spots.
Pátio do Colégio
The birthplace of São Paulo, this reconstructed Jesuit chapel and courtyard marks the exact spot where the city was founded in 1554.

train.note: Brazil has virtually no long-distance passenger trains — rail around São Paulo is commuter-only (Metro/CPTM). For intercity and international overland travel use long-distance buses from the Tietê terminal, or fly.

bus.note: International coaches leave from Terminal Rodoviário do Tietê, South America's biggest bus station. These are marathon rides — well over 24 hours, with border stops — so bring your passport and food money; semi-bed (semi-leito) or bed (leito) seats are worth it.

ferry.note: São Paulo is inland, about 80 km from the sea — no ferry services. The nearest port, Santos, handles cruise ships but has no scheduled international passenger ferries.

half.name: Santos
half.blurb: Historic port city with a lively beachfront, coffee heritage, and a stilt-house museum.

half.name: Guarujá
half.blurb: Popular beach getaway with wide sandy shores and warm Atlantic waters.

half.name: São Roque
half.blurb: Countryside wine route dotted with vineyards, cellars, and rustic hillside restaurants.

half.name: Embu das Artes
half.blurb: Colonial arts town famed for handicraft markets, galleries, and cobblestone streets.

half.name: Holambra
half.country: Near Campinas, São Paulo State, Brazil
half.blurb: Dutch-founded flower capital bursting with tulips, windmills, and colorful spring festivals.
